newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek '97 fx policy to be stable, inflation-minded.
newsitem.headline: Greek '97 fx policy to be stable, inflation-minded.

text.p: ATHENS, Jan 31 - The Bank of Greece will pursue a stable but more flexible foreign exchange policy this year to curb inflation to 4.5 percent by yearend and below 3.0 percent by the end of 1998, the central bank's governor said on Friday.

"The policy for the foreign exchange rate of the drachma is defined by the top priority of curbing inflation," said Bank of Greece governor Lucas Papademos. "Specifically, the stability of the foreign exchange rate of the drachma against the currencies that make up the ecu will be the main goal of monetary policy."
In 1996, the drachma slipped 1.0 percent against the ecu and 3.0 percent in 1995.

He added, "the direction of foreign exchange policy will remain definitely anti-inflationary, but its execution will be characterised by greater flexibility than in the past, taking into consideration the inflationary pressures as well as the prevailing conditions in money and forex markets."
Bank of Greece figures showed imported wholesale price inflation in negative territory, registering a 0.6-percent drop year-on-year in November 1996.

The so-called hard drachma policy, which limits the dollar's slide against the ecu and other European Monetary System (EMS) currencies by less than inflation differentials justify, has been instrumental in reducing inflation.

The central bank's credibility from the hard drachma policy and interest rate differentials favouring the drachma have attracted huge capital inflows, which have beefed up foreign exchange reserves and boosted interbank liquidity.

To sterilise the foreign exchange inflows, the central bank has been draining excess interbank liquidity to prevent it from spilling over to the rest of the economy, threatening its intermediate monetary goals and fuelling inflation.
Limited progress in addressing fiscal imbalances has forced monetary and foreign exchange policy to bear the burden of the fight against inflation.
Asked when the drachma will join the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), Papademos said it was still early to set an ERM entry date.
"It is premature," he said. "Anyway, we will have a new ERM at the begining of 1999."
He added that the ERM entry date was linked to developments in inflation and other economic indicators.
The drachma is not part of the current ERM, but government officials have said it will join as soon as economic conditions allowed.
Greece hopes to be in the second wave of European Union (EU) countries joining EMU. Countries aspiring to enter EMU should have their currencies spend at least two years in the ERM currency grid.
Asked if a rising dollar would alter foreign exchange policy, Papademos said it could happen if excessive dollar swings threatened the country's inflation goal.
He said the dollar/drachma rate mostly followed the dollar's moves against other major currencies in international markets. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
